Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP

Time: ~20 minutes (+ Q&A) • Audience: mixed (epidemiology/biostats) • Presenter: Alexander van Twisk

Slide 1: Aim & objectives

Visual(s): Target + checklist (or a simple timeline showing sections with time budget: Why simulate → ADEMP → Worked example → Pitfalls → Checklist).

Text on screen:

  • Aim: Equip you to design, run, and report a transparent simulation study using ADEMP.
  • By the end, you will be able to:
    1. Explain each ADEMP component and how they connect.
    2. Specify a realistic data‑generating mechanism and a clear estimand.
    3. Build a small power‑by‑simulation in Quarto/R.
    4. Report bias, coverage, and power with Monte Carlo SEs.
    5. Avoid common pitfalls and use the ADEMP table & checklist.

Text to speak: State one overarching aim and four–five actionable objectives (use strong verbs: explain, specify, build, report, avoid). Flag tangible takeaways: a Quarto starter deck, an ADEMP reporting table template, and a one‑page checklist.

Slide 2: Title & hook

Visual(s): Split image: left = messy, ad‑hoc code/printouts; right = clean, staged pipeline (ADEMP). Or a simple ADEMP wheel icon.

Text on screen (minimal):

  • Design & report simulation studies the smart way
  • ADEMP = Aims • Data • Estimands • Methods • Performance
  • Alexander van Twisk • MSc Biostatistics • Stellenbosch | Scigenix

Text to speak: “Formulas are great—until real data get messy. ADEMP helps us design simulations that reflect reality and are easy to reproduce.” Say what the audience will get: a checklist, clear visuals, and a Quarto template.

Slide 3: Why simulate?

Visual(s): 2×2 grid: (closed‑form works / doesn’t) × (assumptions hold / don’t). Icons for nonlinearity, missingness, censoring, clustering.

Text on screen:

  • Study bias, coverage, robustness
  • When formulas are too strict or unavailable
  • Build intuition for design choices

Text to speak: Give one relatable case (e.g., small N with dropout). The goal isn’t to avoid math—it’s to model realistic data‑generating conditions we actually expect.

Slide 4: ADEMP overview

Visual(s): Flow or wheel: A → D → E → M → P, with a 2–3 word example under each.

Text on screen:

  • Aims → precise question
  • Data → how data are generated
  • Estimands → what we target
  • Methods → what we compare
  • Performance → how we judge

Text to speak: ADEMP is a simple order of operations. Aims drive Data and Estimands. Methods must answer the Estimand. Performance measures must match the Aims.

Slide 5: A = Aims

Visual(s): Question cards: Power? Bias? Coverage? Robustness? Sample size?

Text on screen:

  • State primary and secondary aims
  • Confirmatory vs exploratory
  • Pre‑specify scenarios and contrasts

Text to speak: Clarity up front prevents drifting goals. Example: “Find N for 80% power with 10% dropout; also assess sensitivity to 2% misclassification.”

Slide 6: D = Data‑generating mechanisms

Visual(s): Factorial grid heatmap (e.g., event rate × dropout × misclassification). Small timeline for censoring/intervals.

Text on screen:

  • Choose core parameters and realistic ranges
  • Use factorial grids to cover combinations
  • Include stress tests, not just best‑case

Text to speak: Spell out baseline truths (e.g., control risk p0, treatment effect) and nuisance features (dropout, clustering). Factorial designs prevent cherry‑picking scenarios.

Slide 7: E = Estimands

Visual(s): Mini‑table: estimand → parameter (risk difference Δ, log‑odds β, hazard ratio θ, median ratio).

Text on screen:

  • Define the target clearly
  • Align with the scientific question
  • Estimand ≠ estimator (don’t conflate)

Text to speak: Different estimands answer different questions. Decide first: population risk difference or conditional log‑odds? That choice guides methods.

Slide 8: M = Methods

Visual(s): Fairness checklist: same tuning budget, same preprocessing, same convergence rules, same numerical precision, set seeds. Small failure‑handling flow.

Text on screen:

  • Comparable tuning and diagnostics
  • Parity in implementation details
  • Predefine failure/timeout rules

Text to speak: Neutral comparisons require symmetry. Example: one retry on non‑convergence, then record as failure. Report failure rates, not just successes.

Slide 9: P = Performance measures

Visual(s): Small multiples: bias, RMSE, coverage, power, runtime. Include MCSE error bars or ribbons.

Text on screen:

  • Bias, RMSE, Coverage, Power
  • Monte Carlo SEs show precision
  • Look for stable patterns across scenarios

Text to speak: Always include MCSEs so we know if differences are meaningful. Example: MCSE(power) ≈ sqrt(p(1−p)/R).

Slide 10: Worked example — the question + the formula method

Visual(s): Left: equation card with the closed‑form sample size for a two‑sample test of proportions (equal allocation). Right: sticky‑note list of assumptions (no dropout, no misclassification, large‑sample normality, equal variance approximation, fixed p0).

Text on screen:

  • Question: Find N for 80% power (α = 0.05) to detect Δ = p1 − p0 = −0.05.
  • Closed‑form (normal approximation, two‑sample proportions): N_per_arm ≈ ((z_{1−α/2} + z_{1−β})^2 × [p0(1−p0) + p1(1−p1)]) / (p1 − p0)^2
  • Plug‑in example (no dropout): α = 0.05, power = 0.80, p0 = 0.25 ⇒ p1 = 0.20 ⇒ N per arm ≈ 1,090.
  • Why this is insufficient in practice: (1) ignores 10% dropout and 2% misclassification; (2) fragile to the chosen p0; (3) relies on large‑sample normality; (4) cannot target alternative estimands (e.g., marginal RD with covariate adjustment); (5) yields a single N with no MCSE.

Text to speak: Walk through the closed‑form calculation so the audience sees the standard “textbook N.” Then pivot: these assumptions rarely hold. Our simulation will build dropout and misclassification into the data‑generating mechanism, compare two analysis methods (logistic Wald test and prop.test), and return a power curve with MCSE ribbons so we can select an N* that’s robust across plausible scenarios.

Slide 11: Worked example — ADEMP table

Visual(s): Compact ADEMP table, one row per letter.

Text on screen:

  • A: Power ≥ 0.80 for Δ = −0.05
  • D: p0 ∈ {0.15, 0.25}; dropout 10%; misclass 2%
  • E: Population risk difference
  • M: Logistic model Wald test; also prop.test
  • P: Power ± MCSE; bias of Δ-hat; type I error at Δ = 0

Text to speak: Walk row‑by‑row. Primary factors are pre‑set; sensitivity runs extend the grid.

Slide 12: Worked example — loop logic (graphic instead of code)

Visual(s): Flow: start → generate data → fit methods → record metrics → repeat R times → summarise. Tiny code caption only.

Text on screen:

  • R = 2,000 (targets MCSE(power) ≈ 0.01 when p ≈ 0.8)
  • N per arm = 80…400
  • Record: power, bias, coverage, runtime

Text to speak: Narrate the loop. Mention set seeds, config files, logging, and consistent handling of failures/timeouts. Explain why R = 2,000: choose R so Monte Carlo uncertainty is small enough for decisions. For power, MCSE ≈ sqrt[p(1−p)/R]; if p ≈ 0.8 and we want MCSE ≈ 0.01, then R ≥ 0.8×0.2/0.01^2 ≈ 1,600, so we use 2,000 to cover other scenarios and keep MCSEs for bias and coverage acceptably small without excessive runtime.

Slide 13: Worked example — results (power curve)

Visual(s): Power vs N with MCSE ribbon; mark 80% threshold and chosen N*.

Text on screen:

  • Choose N* with a small safety margin
  • Also report nearest smaller/greater N

Text to speak: Show how dropout and misclassification push N upward compared to closed‑form. The ribbon shows uncertainty from finite R.

Slide 14: Worked example — sensitivity & robustness

Visual(s): Small multiples: (A) p0 = 0.15 vs 0.25; (B) dropout = 0%, 5%, 10%.

Text on screen:

  • Scenario choice affects N*
  • Prefer N that is robust over plausible ranges

Text to speak: Point assumptions are brittle. ADEMP encourages looking across a grid and picking designs that behave well, not just at one point.

Slide 15: Mini use‑case 1 — Model misspecification

Visual(s): Bias vs degree of nonlinearity; compare logistic vs a robust alternative.

Text on screen:

  • Purpose: quantify bias when link is wrong
  • Takeaway: use diagnostics; consider robust methods

Text to speak: Show a case where the logit link is wrong. Simulation tells us the size of the problem and when a different method pays off.

Slide 16: Mini use‑case 2 — Neutral method comparison

Visual(s): Dot plot of RMSE/coverage across methods with equal tuning budgets (e.g., MICE vs missForest; or Cox PH vs flexible parametric).

Text on screen:

  • Equal tuning and rules for all methods
  • Report wins, trade‑offs, and failures

Text to speak: Method A rarely “wins everywhere.” Show trade‑offs: accuracy, coverage, speed, and failure rate—all under symmetric conditions.

Slide 17: Mini use‑case 3 — Interval‑censored survival

Visual(s): Interval scheme (Ai, Bi] timeline; small grid of coverage for log‑logistic vs semiparametric interval methods.

Text on screen:

  • Estimand: HR or difference in median survival
  • Methods: icenReg and parametric/semiparametric fits

Text to speak: Complex censoring is manageable with ADEMP: clear estimands + a grid of realistic scenarios.

Slide 18: Pitfalls & questionable practices

Visual(s): Red‑flag stickers: selective scenarios, seed shopping, unfair tuning, hidden failures, no MCSEs.

Text on screen:

  • Pre‑specify; register when possible
  • Keep tuning symmetric; report failures
  • Always include MCSEs

Text to speak: Name the common traps and how to avoid them. Replication and sharing code/data cut down on questionable practices.

Slide 19: Reporting & visuals that work

Visual(s): Gallery: ADEMP table, factorial heatmap, bias/coverage small multiples, power curve with ribbons.

Text on screen:

  • Put ADEMP table in Methods
  • Prefer plots for pattern finding
  • Share code, seeds, and session info

Text to speak: Good visuals + a short ADEMP table make results easy to read and reproduce. Reviewers love clarity.

Slide 20: Practical checklist & resources

Visual(s): Checklist card (8–10 items) + QR to your Quarto repo/template.

Text on screen (checklist):

  • Aims defined and prioritised
  • Factorial scenarios set
  • Estimands explicit
  • Methods tuned fairly
  • Failures handled consistently
  • Metrics + MCSEs reported
  • Code, seeds, session info saved
  • ADEMP table included

Text to speak: Close with the checklist and invite the audience to reuse your Quarto starter.

Slide 21: Q&A (+ backup)

Visual(s): Minimal “Questions?”; QR to repo; contact line.

Text on screen:

  • Questions?
  • alexander.vtwisk@… | GitHub | Scigenix

Text to speak: Invite questions; mention targeted backup slides if people want details.

Backup slides (as needed)

  1. MCSE quick formulas — MCSE(power) ≈ sqrt(p(1−p)/R); MCSE(bias) via sample SD divided by sqrt(R), etc.
  2. Factorial design — full vs fractional; Latin hypercube sketch.
  3. Failure handling — retry limits, logging, exclusion rules.
  4. Code skeleton — minimal R pseudo with seeds and logging.
  5. ADEMP reporting table template — copy‑paste into manuscripts.
  6. References — key peer‑reviewed sources.

Quarto notes (revealjs)

YAML starter:

format:
  revealjs:
    theme: [default]
    slide-number: true
    incremental: true
    transition: fade
    touch: true
    chalkboard: true
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
fig-cap-location: bottom
code-overflow: wrap

Tips:

  • Use two‑column layouts for plot + bullets.
  • Keep on‑slide text short; let plots carry the message.
  • Store SVG icons (ADEMP wheel, checklist) in resources/.
  • Use the menu plugin for quick navigation.
  • Centralise seeds/config; write outputs to outputs/ for reproducibility.
